course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.description: Follow Native American societies, European exploration, the Columbian Exchange, and the Spanish empire from 1491 to 1607.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest
lesson.summary: What crossed the Atlantic after 1492, how epidemics and alliances made Spanish conquest possible, and how American silver and new business methods changed Europe's economy.
learningGoals: Explain the causes of the Columbian Exchange and its effects on Europe and the Americas.
Explain how epidemics, Indigenous alliances, and Spanish weapons contributed to the conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires.
Explain how American silver, new crops, and joint-stock companies helped change Europe's economy.
lesson.bigIdea: The Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals, and diseases between hemispheres. It strengthened European economies while devastating Native populations, and it made Spanish conquest possible.
lesson.context: This topic asks you to read claims about the Exchange and conquest. When you meet a source, ask what it claims, what evidence supports the claim, and what other factors it leaves out.

sections.title: What crossed the Atlantic

blocks.text: The Columbian Exchange was the movement of plants, animals, diseases, and people between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres that followed Columbus's voyages beginning in 1492. From the Americas came maize, potatoes, tomatoes, beans, cacao, and tobacco. From the Old World came wheat, sugar cane, horses, pigs, cattle, and sheep, along with diseases such as smallpox, measles, and influenza.

Potatoes and maize gave European farmers more food from the same land, which stimulated population growth. In the Americas, livestock changed how land was used, and wandering cattle and pigs sometimes damaged Native fields. Horses would later transform life for peoples of the Great Plains.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: Voyages carried crops to Europe, and Europe's food supply and population grew. Voyages also carried diseases to the Americas, and Native populations fell sharply.

sections.takeaway: The Exchange changed both hemispheres, but it did not affect them equally.

sections.title: Epidemics and Spanish conquest

blocks.text: Native peoples had no earlier exposure to Old World diseases, so epidemics spread quickly. In many regions most of the population died within a few generations. These losses weakened Native societies and made conquest easier.

In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with several hundred Spaniards, horses, and steel weapons. He won allies, such as the Tlaxcalans, who resented Aztec tribute demands. Smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in 1520, and the city fell in 1521. In the 1530s Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire, which had been weakened by disease and a civil war.

Spanish expeditions also reached what is now the United States. Ponce de León sailed to Florida in 1513, Hernando de Soto crossed the Southeast in 1539–1542, and Francisco Vázquez de Coronado explored the Southwest in 1540–1542. In 1565 Spain founded St. Augustine in Florida, the oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the continental United States.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Disease did not make conquest automatic. Spanish victories also depended on Indigenous allies, divisions among Native states, and Spanish weapons and horses.

sections.takeaway: Epidemics, Indigenous allies, and Spanish weapons together explain the fall of the Aztec and Inca empires.

sections.title: Silver, trade, and a changing European economy
sections.conceptTitle: Silver, trade, and a changing European economy

blocks.text: Spanish colonists found rich silver deposits at Potosí in the Andes, beginning in 1545, and at Zacatecas in Mexico. Silver flowed to Spain and then across Europe and to Asia, financing armies and expanding trade.

New methods of doing business spread too. Joint-stock companies let investors pool money for risky overseas ventures and share profits. Along with American crops and mineral wealth, these changes helped drive Europe's shift from feudalism, an economy built on land and obligations between lords and peasants, toward capitalism, an economy built on markets, money, and investment. The shift was gradual and uneven.

sections.takeaway: American silver and new business methods helped move Europe toward a market economy.

connections.title: Conquest creates a new labor system
connections.body: Conquest gave Spain control of land and Native workers. Topic 1.5 explains how the encomienda, African slavery, and the caste system organized work and society in the Spanish empire.
connections.transferQuestion: How did the decline of Native populations after epidemics affect the labor systems Spain created?
connections.feedback: A strong answer links population loss to labor shortages and then to the turn toward enslaved Africans.
